summary: Helmuth von Glasenapp worked in Indology, religious studies, and Buddhist studies. He studied at Tübingen, Munich, Berlin, and Bonn under Hermann Jacobi, Richard von Garbe, and Wanczura. He held posts at Bonn, Berlin, Königsberg (1928–1944), and Tübingen (1946–1959).

Sinologist and Buddhist studies scholar Helwig Schmidt-Glintzer studied at the University of Göttingen (~1967–1968) and the University of Munich (~1968–1972). He held academic posts at the University of Munich (~1979–1993) and the University of Göttingen (~1993–2014).

Hemchandra Raychaudhuri was an Indologist and historian. He served as Carmichael Professor and Head of the Department of Ancient Indian History and Culture at the University of Calcutta (attested 1939 and 1965).

Henepola Gunaratana studied at Vidyasekhara and Vidyalankara Pirivenas, Buddhist Missionary College, and American University. In Buddhist studies and philosophy, he served at the Buddhist Institute of Kuala Lumpur, Washington Buddhist Vihara, and American University, and founded the Bhavana Society.

Heng Sure, a scholar of Buddhist and religious studies, studied at Oakland University, UC Berkeley, and the Graduate Theological Union under Ronald Y. Nakasone and Hsuan Hua. He held professorships at Dharma Realm Buddhist University, Bond University, and GTU.

Henk Blezer is a scholar of Tibetology, Buddhist studies, and Indology. He studied at Leiden University (1987–1997), where he later worked as a postdoctoral researcher (1993–1997) and teacher (2002–2008), in addition to working at the IIAS (1997–2001).

Indologist Henk Bodewitz earned classical languages, Indo-Iranian, and PhD degrees at Utrecht University under Jan Gonda. He served at Utrecht as assistant professor (1966) and chair of Sanskrit (1976–1992), and at Leiden University as associate professor and professor (1992–2002).

Henri Bergson was a philosopher who studied at Lycée Condorcet, École Normale Supérieure (~1878–1881), and the University of Paris (~1888–1889). He held positions at the Lycée David d'Angers (~1881–1883) and the Collège de France (1900–1904).

Henri Cordier worked in sinology and history/archaeology after studying at Lycée Chaptal. He held professorships at the Institut national des langues et civilisations orientales (~1881–1925) and Sciences Po (~1886–1925).

Henri Gaidoz studied at Collège Louis-le-Grand and under Albrecht Weber (1865). He taught geography and ethnography at Sciences Po (1872–1908) and served as Directeur d’études in Celtic philology at the École Pratique des Hautes Études (1876).

Henri Hubert, a scholar of religious studies and history/archaeology, studied at Collège Louis-le-Grand and École Normale Supérieure. He held posts at the National Archaeological Museum (~1898–1927), École Pratique des Hautes Études (~1901–1927), and École du Louvre (~1906–1927).

Henri Maspero was a sinologist, linguist, and historian of religion who studied under Édouard Chavannes. He held posts at the École Française d'Extrême-Orient, Collège de France (1918–1945), University of Paris (~1920–1944), and École Pratique des Hautes Études (~1927–1944).
Henri Massé was an Iranian and Central Asian studies scholar and linguist. He held academic posts at the University of Algiers (~1916–1927) and the École des Langues Orientales (~1927–1958).

Historian Henri Pirenne studied at the University of Liège, Berlin, Leipzig, Paris, EPHE, and Ghent. He taught at the University of Liège (~1885–1886) and served as Professor of History at Ghent University (1886–1931).

Henrik Samuel Nyberg worked in Iranian and Central Asian studies, linguistics, and religious studies. He studied at Uppsala University, taught at Fjellstedt School (~1916–1919), and served as docent and professor of Semitic studies at Uppsala University (~1919–1956).

Henry Beveridge was an Indologist and historian. He studied at the University of Glasgow (~1853–1857) and Queen's University Belfast (1856), served in the Indian Civil Service (1857–1893), and was President of The Asiatic Society (1890–1891).

Henry Chung-hung Shiu is a Buddhist studies and philosophy scholar. He studied at the University of Toronto (PhD, 2006) and was taught by Shek-wing Tam, Leonard C. D. C. Priestley, David Waterhouse, and Willard Gurdon Oxtoby.

Henry Clarke Warren worked in Buddhist studies and Indology. He studied at Harvard, Johns Hopkins, and Oxford, working under Charles Rockwell Lanman, Maurice Bloomfield, and T. W. Rhys Davids. He also founded the Harvard Oriental Series in 1891.

Henry George Keene studied at Fort William College and Sidney Sussex College, Cambridge. In the fields of Indology and Iranian and Central Asian studies, he was a fellow at Sidney Sussex (1817) and professor at East India Company College (1824–1834).

Henry Hamilton Hadley studied at Yale, Union Theological Seminary, and Andover Theological Seminary. A scholar of religious studies and linguistics, he served as instructor and professor of Hebrew at Union Theological Seminary and held a Hebrew professorship at Yale Divinity School (1861).
